title: "The Disparities in Food Equality between the East and West Side of the River"

# Introduction

Today is my first day as an assistant teacher for *FoodPrints*, an organization that helps combat food inequities by teaching kids in elementary schools how to sustain themselves. As I sit on the blue line Metro to Eastern Market in Ward 6, I'm reminded of a few sources I viewed recently displaying food access disparities between the east and west sides of the Anacostia river. 

## Grocery Stores

![Figure 1. Map of Grocery Stores in DC (2023)](images/Grocery_Store_Map.png)

Yesterday, I completed an assignment on the map above for the class at my university which put me through the FoodPrints program &mdash; Hands-On Food Education in the **Global Food Institute Department** &mdash; and it was evident that grocery stores fell short on the east side. Moreover, I found an all-or-nothing phenomenon; many areas of the East side contained no grocery stores, while other areas boasted several grocery stores stacked on top of each other. This is a common trend on this map, where services are not well distributed among the District, but rather huddled together where the stores can maximize profit. The focus is not on giving residents access to resources.

![Figure 2. DC Transit on Google Maps](images/DC_Transit_Map.png)

To make matters worse, transit on the East side is significantly restricted. As seen in Figure 2, the green line is essentially the only Metro rail in the part of Southeast DC east of the river, with most areas at least a mile away from a station. This significantly worsens the previous issue, as residents are forced to walk the long distance to these grocery stores.

# Community-Oriented Solutions

It is unlikely that these grocery store conglomerates will address these disparities. Therefore, solutions should prioritize working within the community.

## FoodPrints Schools

FoodPrints is arguably the best example of a community-oriented solution due to its incorporation of gardens and group-cooking lessons. Furthermore, the most impoverished schools carry farm stands, places requested by the communities where families can buy fresh, affordable produce. I encountered a much better distribution across D.C. [here](https://www.freshfarm.org/foodprints/schools).

```{r}
library(ggplot2)
df <- data.frame(
  Ward = c("Ward 1", "Ward 2", "Ward 3", "Ward 4", "Ward 5", "Ward 6", "Ward 7", "Ward 8"),
  Region = c(rep("West of River", 6), rep("East of River", 2)),
  Schools = c(1, 1, 0, 3, 3, 6, 3, 3)
  )
ggplot(df, aes(x = Ward, y = Schools, fill = Region)) +
  geom_col() +
  labs(
    x = "Ward",
    y = "Number of Schools",
    fill = "Region",
    title = "FoodPrints Schools by Ward"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

mean_east_of_river <- (3+3)/2
mean_west_of_river <- (round)((1+1+0+3+3+6)/6, digits = 2)
```

The average amount of schools per ward east of the river was slightly greater than the average of those west of the river, at `r mean_east_of_river` and `r mean_west_of_river` respectively. Still, because of the grocery store deficit, I feel that there should be a larger focus on Wards 7 and 8. The distribution doesn't need to be proportionate. Ward 6 already proves this, holding 6 of the schools in the program, compared to 1-3 schools in other wards.

## Farmers' Markets

Farmers' markets are another community-oriented solution, and [this map](https://opendata.dc.gov/datasets/DCGIS::farmers-market-locations/explore?location=38.893812%2C-77.020955%2C12) again displays an even distribution across the District. However, there are a few downsides to farmers' markets: 

- They tend to be less convenient, open less days of the week.
- The prices are often more expensive due to their inability to monopolize on supply chains in the same way that grocery stores do.

Still, they are fresh, sustainable ways to be fed by members of the community. With the limited options available, these can be a significant upgrade for residents of poor districts.

# Conclusion

The food inequities on the east side of the river cause significant harm to those who live there. It is a never-ending cycle, where poverty creates unequal access to resources, and that unequal access contributes to higher rates of poverty. However, community-oriented solutions do three important things to close this gap:

1. They prioritize providing residents with access to resources over the making of profit, 
2. They take direct feedback from the community, 
3. They are evenly distributed, based on communities desire for fresh food rather than where the best consumers are.

Therefore, while farmers' markets and FoodPrints cannot completely replace the void left by grocery stores, expanding these community services is essential to decreasing the food equity gap between those on the west and east side of the Anacostia river.
